title: Aubergine unagi
creator: @ricesprinkles
intro: An aubergine steamed until it gives way, flattened, seared and then glazed in a sweet soy sauce until it shines, in the manner of grilled eel. Spoon it over rice for a supper that asks for very little shopping and very little washing up.

ingredients.text: A splash of fish sauce (optional; amount not given)
Spring onions, chopped, to garnish (amount not given)

steps.text: Cut the aubergine across into pieces about 15 cm long. Steam them over a high (8-9) heat for about 10 minutes, until a knife slides in with no resistance.
Leave the pieces to cool until you can handle them.
Stir together 1 tbsp dark soy sauce, 1/2 tbsp light soy sauce, 1 tbsp mirin, 1 tsp sugar, the fish sauce if using, 1 tsp cornflour and 120 ml water, until the cornflour has dissolved.
Halve each piece lengthways. Make shallow cuts across the flesh without going through the skin, then press gently with the back of a knife to flatten it into an eel-like fillet.
Heat 1 tbsp oil in a large frying pan over medium-high (7). Lay the aubergine in skin-side down and cook until lightly browned.
Turn the pieces over and cook until the flesh is golden. A little char is no harm.
Turn the heat to medium (5-6). Pour in the sauce and simmer, turning the aubergine halfway, until the sauce has reduced to a sticky glaze that coats it.
Lay it over a bowl of rice and scatter with furikake and chopped spring onions. Eat while hot.

to_check: Frying times are not given by the creator, only "lightly browned", "golden" and "mostly reduced"; the 10 minutes steaming is from the website. Total time per website: 25 minutes.
The caption lists the aubergine as "1 large Asian eggplant"; the website cuts it into 6-inch (15 cm) lengths. The video shows it flattened and the website adds scoring, which I have followed.
"Dark soy sauce" and "light soy sauce" are both listed as "soy sauce" in the ingredient names.
Furikake and spring onion amounts are not given.
notes: Leave out the fish sauce for a vegan version; check the furikake too, as many contain bonito or other fish.
A little shichimi togarashi or a soft egg on top would not be out of place.

title: Baked curd cheese casserole
creator: @kristina_pesik
intro: Somewhere between a baked cheesecake and a set custard: soft, creamy and only just sweet. Everything goes into one bowl and is blended smooth, and it is better still the next morning, cold from the fridge or warmed a slice at a time.

ingredients.text: 655 g curd cheese, 6% fat (Russian tvorog; quark is the closest UK match)
355 ml cream, 20% fat (single cream is the nearest)
Vanilla extract, to taste (amount not given)
Lime zest, to taste (amount not given)

steps.text: Heat the oven to 160°C fan and line a baking dish with baking paper.
Tip the curd cheese, cream cheese and cream into a large bowl and blend until completely smooth, with no lumps of curd left.
Add the sugar and eggs, then the vanilla and finely grated lime zest, tasting as you go if you like.
Sift or sprinkle in the cornflour (it holds the casserole together) and blend again until the batter is smooth and pourable.
Pour the batter into the lined dish and bake for about 1 hour, until the top is a good golden brown and the middle no longer wobbles when you nudge the dish. Ovens vary, so go by the look of it.
Take it out and leave it to cool a little before cutting. Eat it warm, or chill it overnight and warm a slice the next morning.

to_check: Oven: caption says 180°C, top and bottom heat (conventional), about 1 hour. Converted to 160°C fan (conventional minus 20).
Dish size and depth are not stated; the video shows a rectangular dish. Servings are not given.
Vanilla and lime zest are "to taste" in the original, with no amount.
Eggs are given as 260 g, "about 5" in the caption; five large eggs is an estimate.
"Cream 20%" is a Russian grade; single cream (about 18%) is the closest everyday UK cream.
prep_min 15 is an estimate; the creator gives no prep time.
Translated from Russian.
notes: The creator likes it best after a night in the fridge, a slice cut and warmed for breakfast.
Curd cheese (tvorog) is drier and more crumbly than UK cottage cheese. If you can only find cottage cheese, drain it well and blend it first; this is a swap, not what the creator used.

title: Basque cheesecake
creator: @soohyunlees
intro: A cheesecake with no base to blind-bake and no water bath, just a hot oven and a deeply browned top over a custard the colour of butter. It is better after a night or two in the fridge, so make it the day before you want it.

ingredients.text: 650 g cream cheese (block), cut into cubes, at room temperature
250 ml whipping cream, at room temperature
Baking parchment, for lining a 20 cm cake tin

steps.text: Set the oven to 220°C fan. Line a 20 cm cake tin with baking parchment, letting it stand a little above the rim.

Put the 650 g cream cheese cubes, 195 g sugar, 1 tsp vanilla, 4 g cornflour and 2 g salt into a food processor. Blend on a low speed until smooth, stopping to scrape down the sides and bottom now and then so nothing hides. (An even mixture is what keeps the cake smooth.)
Pour in the 180 g eggs and mix on low until completely combined.
Pour in the 250 ml whipping cream and mix slowly until the batter is well combined and pourable.
Pour the batter through a fine sieve into the lined tin, to catch any lumps.
Tap the tin on the work surface a few times to knock out the air bubbles.
Bake at 210°C fan for 23-25 minutes. It is ready when the top is deep brown and the centre still wobbles like set jelly when you nudge the tin.
Leave the cake in its tin on a wire rack until it reaches room temperature.
Cover and chill overnight. Lift out by the parchment, cut into wedges and eat cold, with a fork and no ceremony.

to_check: Oven temperatures conflict inside the caption: step 1 says preheat to 240C, step 4 says bake at 230C. I have used the conversions of both as written (240C becomes 220°C fan, 230C becomes 210°C fan), assuming the creator's figures are conventional, not fan. If your oven runs hot, the top may darken faster than the 23-25 min suggests; watch it.
8 inch cake pan converted to 20 cm.
250 g whipping cream given by weight; I have written 250 ml (an estimate, as cream is slightly lighter than water).
180 g eggs is about 3 medium eggs (estimate); weigh them out after beating.
Servings not given. Prep and total times are not given; prep_min is an estimate, total_min left blank because of the overnight chill.
Cornflour is gluten-free by itself; check the label of the cream cheese and vanilla if gluten matters.
No speech in the video; everything comes from the caption and frames.
notes: No food processor: the creator says it can be made by hand or in a stand mixer, as long as everything is at room temperature.
It keeps improving in the fridge for a couple of days.
Serve with strong black coffee.

title: Brie and pear filo tart
creator: @guinda.guindilla
intro: Sheets of filo folded into accordions and stood on end in a tray, with slices of soft cheese and pear tucked between the folds, set with a savoury custard. It should be eaten soon after baking, while the pastry is crisp, and a thread of honey over the top finishes it.

ingredients.text: 1 packet filo pastry (weight and sheet count not given)
About 10 slices of brie or camembert-style cheese (weight not given)
200 ml cooking cream (or rice or oat cream)
Salt and black pepper, to taste
A few fresh thyme leaves (amount not given)
Honey (or agave or maple syrup), to taste

steps.text: Set the oven to 180°C fan (the caption says to preheat for about 15 minutes).
Take the filo sheets two at a time and fold each pair concertina-style into an accordion.
Stand the folded filo on end in a baking tray lined with baking paper, packed close together so they hold each other upright. A tray that fits snugly works best.
Brush the filo with the melted butter.
Slice the cheese and the pear thinly, so that the slices fit between the folds of pastry.
Tuck the cheese and pear slices alternately into the folds, spreading them evenly over the tray.
Beat the 2 eggs with the cream and season with salt and pepper. Pour this over the tart, spreading it so that it soaks in everywhere.
Scatter over the thyme leaves.
Bake at 160°C fan for about 40 minutes, until the custard is set and the filo is deep golden.
Cool the tray on a wire rack. Finish with a thin thread of honey and eat while it is still crisp.

to_check: Missing quantities: filo packet weight or number of sheets, cheese weight (only "about 10 slices"), thyme, honey (to taste) and the size of the baking tray.

Oven temperatures: the caption says preheat to 200 degrees and bake at 180; converted to 180°C fan and 160°C fan, assuming the creator's figures are conventional. Spanish ovens are often fan-assisted, so check how fast it browns.
Cooking cream (nata para cocinar, usually about 18-20% fat) is recorded as single cream, which is the nearest UK equivalent; this is a substitution.
Eggs written "huevos 00" in the caption; I have taken it as plain eggs, size not given.
When the thyme goes on is not stated; I have scattered it on top before baking, which is a guess.
Servings not given; prep and total times are estimates (cook time 40 min is given).
The video says the temperature and time are in the description; they are in the caption (see above).
notes: The creator used Coronat de Mascla Perol, a Catalan cheese, with the pear (from the transcript); brie or camembert is the suggestion in the caption.
Pear can be swapped for figs when they are in season, or for apple.
It is a tart to eat straight away, because the filo softens quickly.

title: Broccolini beans with tinned fish
creator: @justine_snacks
intro: Think spaghetti aglio e olio with the pasta swapped for creamy white beans, and a pile of finely chopped broccolini cooked down into a sauce. A good use for the tin of fish at the back of the cupboard, and for a heel of crusty bread.

ingredients.text: 225 g dried white beans (or drained tinned beans; amount not given)
2 tsp flaky kosher salt, for the soak
1 tbsp flaky kosher salt, for the pot
225 g broccolini (the ingredient list says 340 g; see To check)
120 ml extra-virgin olive oil (the oil from the tin of fish, topped up to 120 ml, works too)
½ tsp flaky kosher salt, and freshly ground black pepper
1 tin (120 g) mackerel, anchovies or sardines

steps.text: Put the dried beans in a large bowl, cover with water by at least 5 cm and stir in the 2 tsp salt. Leave to soak for 6 to 24 hours (the longer they soak, the quicker they cook). Skip to step 8 if you are using tinned beans.
Set a large pot over a medium (5–6) heat and pour in 60 ml olive oil, enough to coat the base. Let it warm for a few minutes.

Peel and halve the onion, leaving the root on. Halve the small lemon lengthways and peel 5 garlic cloves. Lay the onion, lemon and garlic in the oil, cut sides down, and sear for 6–8 minutes until charred, then turn.
Drain the beans and add them to the pot with 1 tbsp salt and 1,400 ml water. Bring to a simmer, cover and cook for 45 minutes to 1 hour.
From 45 minutes on, taste 2 or 3 beans (they can cook unevenly) until they are creamy and tender right through.

Strain off most of the broth, leaving about 120 ml in the pot with the beans. Bin the lemon and keep the onion and garlic with the beans. Save the rest of the broth: it makes a fine stock. Set the pot aside.
Chop 225 g of broccolini very finely. Slice 6 garlic cloves and 4 Calabrian chillies thinly and set aside.

Warm 120 ml olive oil in a large frying pan over a medium (5–6) heat. If you are using the oil from your tin of fish, pour that in first and top up with olive oil to 120 ml. Add 4 anchovy fillets, 1 tsp fennel seeds and 1 tsp oregano and stir for 30–60 seconds, until the anchovies have melted into the oil.
Add the garlic and chillies and let the oil simmer for 3–4 minutes, until the edges of the garlic turn golden.
Add the broccolini and stir to coat. Cook for 6–8 minutes with ½ tsp salt and plenty of black pepper, until it has wilted down to a rough, glossy sauce.
Tip in everything from the bean pot, onion, garlic and broth included (or drained tinned beans), and stir until the beans are well coated.
Break in the tin of fish and stir, breaking it into small pieces. Squeeze in the juice of half a lemon.
Simmer uncovered for 5–6 minutes, until thick with a little oil pooling at the edges.
Taste and add salt, pepper and lemon juice as needed, then stir in 45 g chopped parsley. Eat straight away with crusty bread.

to_check: Broccolini: the ingredient list says 3/4 lb (340 g), but step 7 says to chop 8 oz (225 g). Used 225 g; the page is inconsistent.

Times: the page gives prep 12 hours (soak) and cook 30 minutes, but the beans alone take 45–60 minutes. Page figures are used in the frontmatter; the real cooking time is nearer 75 minutes (my estimate).
Amount of tinned beans is not on the page (it refers to a note that was not captured). Two 400 g tins would be a reasonable guess, but check the original.
Heat settings: the page says only medium for the pot and the pan; hob numbers are my translation to induction (5–6).

Conversions from US: 1/2 lb = 225 g, 1/4 cup = 60 ml, 1/2 cup = 120 ml, 6 cups = 1,400 ml (1.42 l), 4.2 oz tin = 120 g, 1 cup chopped parsley (1.5 oz) = 45 g, 5 oz onion = 140 g, 2 oz lemon = 55 g, 2 inches = 5 cm.
Salt: the page says "1 tablespoon and 2 teaspoons" divided between the soak and the pot; split taken from steps 1 and 4.
The Reel is from the creator's "not buying any more groceries" series and says the website version has changes; the website was followed.
notes: Mackerel, sardines or anchovies all work. The creator likes tins flavoured with lemon, capers, olives or chilli.
Using the oil from the tin as the base oil is the creator's trick in the video: measure it out, then top up with olive oil to 120 ml.
The page names Diamond Crystal, a light, flaky kosher salt. With fine table salt, use roughly half the quantity and taste as you go.
Tinned beans make it a much quicker supper (skip steps 1 to 6).

title: Charred hispi cabbage with whipped miso tofu
creator: @christinasots
intro: Cabbage wedges roasted hard until their edges blacken, then covered to steam until soft and buttery inside. They sit on a cloud of whipped miso tofu with sesame chives and a little crispy chilli oil. Serve with rice and it is a full supper.

ingredients.text: Olive oil, for rubbing (amount not given)
1 tsp flaky sea salt (use less if using table salt)
2 tbsp toasted sesame seeds (black and white)

steps.text: Heat the oven to 200°C fan. Cut the cabbage into 4 wedges, through the core so they hold together.
Rub the wedges all over with olive oil, salt and pepper, then lay them on a baking sheet.
Roast uncovered for 15 minutes, until the edges are charred and crisp.
Cover the tray with foil and turn the oven down to 180°C fan. Return it for a further 10–15 minutes, until a toothpick slides easily through the thickest part.

Meanwhile, blend 1 tbsp of sesame oil, 1 tsp of flaky salt, 1/2 tsp of white miso, 1 tsp of tahini, 1 tsp of rice wine vinegar and 300 g of well-drained silken tofu until perfectly smooth. Chill in the fridge to set a little.
Chop the chives finely and stir them into a bowl with 2 tbsp of sesame seeds and a pinch of salt and pepper.

Spread most of the whipped tofu over a large plate and set the cabbage on top. Spoon over the remaining tofu, drizzle with 1–2 tbsp of crispy chilli oil and scatter with the sesame chives. Serve with rice.

to_check: Oven temperatures: caption gives 220°C then 200°C (conventional); converted to fan by subtracting 20, giving 200°C fan then 180°C fan.
Olive oil amount not given (caption lists sesame oil only, but the method uses olive oil for the cabbage). Salt and pepper for the cabbage and for the chives are "to taste".
The caption's 1 tsp salt appears to be for the whipped tofu; this is an inference.
Rice amount not given. Prep time not given; 30 min is the total from the caption.
notes: Pat the tofu well, or it will make the whip watery.
No blender: mash the tofu through a sieve and beat in the other ingredients, though it will be less smooth.
Fish or veg swap: not needed, this is already vegan.

title: Chilli peanut crispy rice salad with honey soy salmon
creator: @cookwithauds
intro: Day-old rice, dressed and baked until it shatters, then tossed through a green, crunchy salad with a creamy peanut dressing. Honey soy salmon sits on top. A good way to use up cold rice, and a dish that rewards being eaten while the rice is still crisp.

ingredients.text: 60 ml chilli oil with the crispy bits (fried chilli in oil)
450 g salmon fillet, cut into cubes
1 heaping tbsp creamy peanut butter (about 30 g)
1 tbsp chilli oil with the crispy bits
1.5 large cucumbers, diced and patted dry (weight not given)
1 large avocado, cubed, sprinkled with salt and black pepper

steps.text: Heat the oven to 185°C fan. Stir the rice with 30 ml of white vinegar, 1 tsp of sesame oil, 1 tbsp of sugar and 60 ml of chilli oil until every grain is coated.
Spread the rice over a baking tray and bake for 40 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes, until deep golden and crisp.

Meanwhile, put the cubed salmon in a bowl with 60 ml of soy sauce, 2 tbsp of honey, 1 tsp of sesame oil, 1 tsp each of onion powder and garlic powder, 1/2 tsp of salt and 1 tsp of black pepper. Turn gently and leave for at least 10 minutes.
Air fry the salmon at 185°C fan for 10 minutes, until the edges are caramelised and the flesh flakes.

Blend 80 ml of soy sauce, 1 heaping tbsp of honey, 1 heaping tbsp of peanut butter, 1 tbsp of chilli oil, 30 ml of white vinegar and 1 tsp each of onion powder and garlic powder until smooth and creamy.
Toss the cucumber, edamame, spring onions, coriander and avocado together in a large bowl. Add a handful of peanuts.
Fold in the crispy rice and as much dressing as you like, then top with the salmon. Eat straight away, while the rice still crackles.

to_check: No speech (music only), so the caption is the only source. The video also has no spoken method.
Oven and air fryer temperatures: source gives 400°F for both. Converted as 400°F to about 205°C, minus 20 for fan, rounded to 185°C fan. This is an estimate; an air fryer may want 180–200°C.
Assembly is not described in the caption; the order of combining above is a reasonable guess.
Cooked rice weight is converted from 1.5 cups at about 190 g per cup (estimate). Salmon 1 lb is about 450 g.

Cucumber weight is not given ("1.5 large"). Edamame (1 cup, about 150 g), spring onion (1/3 cup, about 30 g) and coriander (1/4 cup, about 15 g) are estimates. Peanut butter 1 heaping tbsp is about 30 g (estimate).
Peanut amount ("handful") not given. Servings and timings (apart from baking and air frying) not given.
"Fried chili in oil" assumed to be chilli crisp / chilli oil with crispy bits.
notes: Day-old rice matters: freshly cooked rice steams rather than crisps.
Keep the dressing separate until the last minute and the rice will stay crunchy for longer.
The salad makes a lunch on its own without the salmon, for a vegetarian version.

title: Cod grenobloise
creator: @adambyatt
intro: A thick fillet of cod, briefly cured so it cooks up firm and seasoned through, sitting on a warm cauliflower purée under a brown butter dressing of capers, lemon and crisp bread. A restaurant dish that is more patience than difficulty, and well worth it for a dinner when you want something a little grand.

ingredients.text: 1 cod fillet (250 g), pin boned and trimmed (serves 2)
100 g butter, in total (50 g for the croutons, 25 g for the braise, 25 g for the sauce)
Olive oil, for frying and finishing (amount not given)
100 ml fish stock (water or white wine if needed)
2 slices sourdough, cut into small dice
Warm cauliflower purée (amount and recipe not given)

steps.text: Mix the 25 g salt and 15 g sugar together and coat the cod fillet evenly all over. Leave it for 12 minutes (the fish firms slightly and turns a little translucent).

Rinse the cod under cold water and pat it very dry. Rest it skin-side down on a tray lined with a clean cloth, with a piece of paper laid lightly over the flesh. For the best skin and sear, leave it uncovered in the fridge overnight instead.
Heat the oven to 140°C fan.
Melt 50 g of the butter in a large frying pan over medium (5–6). Add the diced sourdough and toast, stirring, until golden. Lift the croutons out onto a plate to drain.

Wipe the pan if you need to, then heat a thin layer of olive oil over medium-high (7). Pat the cod dry again and lay it in flesh-side down, pressing it down gently with a weight or the back of a spatula for the first few seconds.
Leave it alone for 6–8 minutes, until the underside is deep golden and the fish lifts away from the pan without sticking (it releases when it is ready).
Lift the cod out carefully into an ovenproof dish, skin-side down. Pour in 100 ml fish stock and dot with 25 g butter.
Braise in the oven for 6–8 minutes, until the flesh is just opaque and flakes at the thickest part, then rest.
In the same frying pan, cook the last 25 g of diced butter over medium (5–6) until golden brown and smelling of toasted nuts (a beurre noisette). Take the pan off the heat.
Pour in the reserved lemon juice and 20 ml white wine, standing back as it spits, and shake the pan until the sauce turns glossy and emulsified.
Stir in 20 g capers and 20 g diced cornichons, then the lemon segments and 20 g parsley.
Fold in the croutons last, so they stay crisp, and season to taste.

Spoon warm cauliflower purée onto warm plates. Peel the skin from the cod and set the fish on top, spoon the garnish over and finish with a thread of olive oil. Eat straight away while the croutons are still crackling.

to_check: The cauliflower purée is shown in the video and mentioned in the caption, but there is no recipe or quantity for it. Make your own, or use about 400 g cauliflower (an estimate, not from the source).
Olive oil amount for frying and finishing is not given.
Oven temperature: the caption says 160°C without saying fan or conventional. I treated it as conventional (160 minus 20 = 140°C fan); if the chef meant fan, use 160°C fan.
Hob heat is not given for the croutons or noisette butter (caption says "medium heat" and "medium-hot oil"). Mapped to medium (5–6) and medium-high (7).
Size of the sourdough dice, resting time after braising and the amount of lemon juice are not given.
Caption says "Serves two people" with a single 250 g fillet; the caption also says to portion into 250 g pieces or individual servings. Treated as one 250 g fillet for 2.
Prep, cook and total times are estimates (the cure takes 12 min; the optional overnight drying is not counted).
The caption mentions no website recipe, so no web lookup was made.
notes: The brief cure means the cod needs no extra salt in the pan. Drying it well, ideally overnight in the fridge, is what gives the crisp, golden finish.
A fish stock cube made up with water will do, or use water or white wine if you have none.
Any thick white fish fillet, such as haddock or hake, would take this garnish.

title: Cod with mustard sauce in paper boats
creator: @just.homemade.food
intro: Baking paper folded into a boat, tied at both ends with string, and filled with ribbons of carrot and courgette, a fillet of cod and a herby mustard sauce. The fish steams in its own juices, and opening the paper at the table is half the pleasure.

ingredients.text: Carrot, cut into thin ribbons (amount not given)
Courgette, cut into thin ribbons (amount not given)
Mustard, wholegrain by the look of it (amount not given)

steps.text: Fold a large sheet of baking paper into a long boat shape, pinch the two ends together and tie each with string. Open the boat out so it holds its shape.
Drizzle a little olive oil in a zigzag along the bottom of the boat.
Lay ribbons of carrot and courgette along the boat, then set the cod fillet on top.
In a small bowl, stir together olive oil, a squeeze of lime juice, chopped dill and mustard until you have a loose green sauce.
Spoon the sauce over the cod so it is covered, then tuck a few cherry tomatoes in around the fish.
Cook the boat in an air fryer until the cod flakes easily with a fork and the tomatoes have split. Temperature and time are not given (see To check).
Bring it to the table in its paper and open it up. Eat the cod with the vegetables and spoon the juices over, while it is still steaming.

The oven suggestion in Notes is mine, not the creator's.

A little more lime at the table sharpens the mustard.

title: Creamy kabocha pumpkin soup
creator: @yukiskitchen
intro: Kabocha, steamed until soft over a little water and a strip of kombu, then blended with silken tofu so the soup turns velvety without any cream. Miso, mirin and sake give it a gentle savoury sweetness, a good bowl for a cold evening once the pumpkin is in the shops.

ingredients.text: 700 g kabocha pumpkin, peeled, seeded and cut into chunks
3 tbsp miso (the creator uses an organic miso; type not given)
Crusty bread or rice, to serve (optional)

steps.text: Scoop the seeds out of the kabocha, then cut it into rough chunks and trim off the skin. It is a bit of work, but worth it.
Pour 500 ml water into a large pot and add the kombu (it lends the soup its savoury depth).
Add the kabocha chunks, put the lid on and steam over a medium heat (5–6) until a cocktail stick slides in easily. Cooking time is not given.
While the kabocha cooks, blend the silken tofu until smooth and creamy. Set it aside.
Lift out the kombu. Blend the kabocha, with its cooking water, to a smooth soup.
Stir in 1 tbsp sake, 1 tbsp mirin and 3 tbsp miso.
Fold in the tofu cream until the soup looks glossy and even.
Ladle into bowls while warm and scatter with toasted pumpkin seeds and chopped chives. Eat with crusty bread or rice.

Heat setting (medium, 5–6) is an assumption; no heat is given.
Whether the kabocha is blended with its cooking water is inferred; the caption just says "blend the kabocha into a smooth soup". Add water to loosen if it is too thick.
No servings, and no amounts for the pumpkin seeds and chives.
The miso type is not stated (the caption names a brand). Listed here as "miso".
No website recipe link in the caption or post data, so none was looked up.
notes: It keeps well in the fridge for a few days, reheated gently. The tofu may thicken it; loosen with a splash of water.
Any miso will do, though a mild white miso keeps the colour bright.

title: Creamy mushroom and miso pasta
creator: @deliciouslyella
intro: A sauce of silken tofu, miso and soaked porcini blended until it turns velvety, then stirred through pasta, browned mushrooms and soft spinach. It is quick, savoury and wonderfully rich without a drop of cream, which makes it a good midweek supper.

ingredients.text: 2 handfuls of spinach (about 60 g), finely sliced
A small bunch of chives (amount not given), chopped

steps.text: Put the dried porcini in a bowl and cover with 150 ml boiling water. Leave for 10 minutes, until soft.
Put the pasta on to cook in well-salted boiling water (heat 9) according to the packet. Drain it, keeping a mugful of the cooking water.

Meanwhile, set a large frying pan over medium-high (7) and add a drizzle of olive oil. Tip in the sliced chestnut mushrooms with a pinch of salt and cook for 5–10 minutes, until tender and starting to colour.
Tip the soaked porcini and their liquid into a blender with the garlic, tofu, miso and lemon juice. Blend until completely smooth, then season to taste.

Add the drained pasta, the sauce, the spinach and the chives to the mushroom pan. Stir over the heat for about a minute, until the spinach wilts, loosening with a little of the reserved pasta water if it seems thick.
Serve in warm bowls with a little sea salt and plenty of black pepper.

to_check: Servings are not given. Judging by 300 g pasta and 600 g mushrooms, it feeds about 3 to 4 (an estimate).
"2 handfuls of spinach" and "small bunch of chives" have no weights; about 60 g spinach is an estimate.
Caption says "½ lemons" and lists it with the sauce ingredients; I took it as the juice of half a lemon.
Caption lists the garlic as "2 cloves" with no prep; they are blended raw.
Prep, cook and total times: the caption claims 15 minutes; I added a little for slicing the mushrooms (estimate).
Pasta water amount and the pack cooking time are not given.

The sauce keeps for a day or two in the fridge; loosen with a splash of water when reheating.

title: Creamy pesto orzo with crispy salmon
creator: @samseats
intro: Orzo cooked slowly with leeks and stock, then stirred through a bright green pesto of spinach, basil and toasted walnuts until it turns creamy and almost risotto-like. Salmon with a crackling skin sits on top. A dinner for two to share, or for four, that looks like far more effort than it is.

ingredients.text: 1 garlic clove (leave it out if you are not sharing the dinner)
Black pepper and sea salt, to season
4 salmon fillets, skin on (weight not given)

title: Roasted aubergine dip
creator: @hungrypaprikas
intro: Cubed aubergine and onion left to melt together in olive oil, tomato and pomegranate molasses, then mashed into a sweet, tangy, faintly spicy dip. It does all the work in the oven, which makes it a sensible thing to have in the fridge when people are coming.

title: Scarpaccia with pepper and onion

intro: A thin, crackling Italian tart, normally made with courgettes, here built almost entirely from sweet peppers and red onions with just enough flour to hold them together. Cut it into squares for a light lunch or a snack, warm or cooled.

Dried rosemary and thyme, to taste
Salt and black pepper, to taste
A little extra polenta, for sprinkling

title: Spaghetti alla Nerano

title: Sticky soy glazed squash with peanut lime sauce
